title: Mount Kimbie - Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Lauren Taylor spoke with Kai Campos of Mount Kimbie about Love What Survives, his creative partnership with Dom Maker and the band's NTS residency. Triple R dates the archive to 7 September 2017, the day before the album's release. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Mount Kimbie have put out a bunch of singles from Love What Survives in the lead-up, including 'We Go Home Together', featuring UK producer and good friend of the band James Blake. As well as James Blake, they've called in King Krule's Archy Marshall and Mica Levi from Micachu and the Shapes.

They're a progressive band, always pushing new musical boundaries with every release. They burst onto the scene around 2008, putting out a couple of EPs, and in 2010 put out their debut album, the critically acclaimed Crooks & Lovers. They were certainly an influential outfit around that time and had a central role in the so-called post-dubstep sound. Many over the years have said Mount Kimbie were responsible for inspiring that term, though I think the band themselves have possibly come out and said otherwise.

The group signed to Warp Records in 2012 and put out their second release, Cold Spring Fault Less Youth. They're also putting out their third album through Warp, due out tomorrow, called Love What Survives. This new record is the product of three years of intense creative development. It came with a lot of challenges, including geographical separation, as Dom Maker is now based in LA, with Kai still living in London. The duo were travelling back and forth to work together on the album, cultivating ideas in intense creative sessions.

Recently the band also did a residency at NTS Radio in London, which was a source of influence in defining the direction of this record. They pulled in a bunch of their mates for these live radio shows, including the album contributors as well as Warpaint, Actress, Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, Connan Mockasin, Julia Holter and many others across that NTS series. The variety of those shows pushed the band to explore new areas, new pieces of kit and new sounds.

The band have said Love What Survives has been a fascinating process that changed them as a band. I began my chat with Kai talking about his experience of putting together the album and why they felt that way.

Kai: I think when you finish a record, in my experience, you have this feeling of freedom and sense that you've figured it out. Suddenly you're in a period where you've almost by definition finished an hour's worth of music and 10 or 12 songs or something like that. And you think, "That's good, I'm never going to struggle to finish music again."

And then life happens and stuff. You find somewhere down the line that you want to be doing something different, and you have those new questions or it's difficult in a new way. I definitely thought after the last one that this third one wouldn't be very difficult to make. And it was definitely the hardest process to crack, to get into.

Every time you end up having to throw away what you think you've learned in the past, I think, to move forward. So it's always interesting in that way and makes you a more well-rounded person and artist in some way.

This one especially was about letting go, for want of a better non-cliché term, of nearly everything that I thought made sense when it came to making music, which is quite a scary thing to do as well. There's always a period where you think, "Oh, this might be crap." Then you inevitably do make some stuff that supports that theory, and you have to find the right action to keep on working regardless until it's not crap.

Lauren: The title is Love What Survives. Mount Kimbie have perhaps, in some way, survived almost 10 years in the music industry and in your creative partnership with Dom. You've both recently turned 30 and probably done a fair bit of growing up in your time together. What are the keys to longevity in a musical partnership, still loving what you do and feeling inspired?

Kai: That's the whole thing. I feel like that's the goal at the end of the day, and nearly everything should be in support of that. It's not always as simple as "follow your dreams", because it gets really complicated. Is your dream to have your music flogged for an advert? But is it also your dream that that advert then pays for six months where you can do far more interesting things that wouldn't be sustainable any other way?

There's things you end up doing that you could be jaded about, but I guess it's a balance of the actual business side of stuff with just writing all the time, which is also not always fun. We've always given each other plenty of space creatively, so there'll be a period where we're off doing our own thing for a long time. Then you have that time to grow individually. It's always really interesting to see where the other person has taken it, or having to explain why you're feeling like this is a cool thing to do.

The real key is actually communication, and good communication, because when you're exhausted it's really hard to do everything as well as you'd like. We definitely, when we were constantly exhausted at the end of the last tour cycle of the last album, were at a point where we weren't communicating very well, so we needed to take a step back. There have been a lot of big heart-to-hearts along this process and getting back to a place where we're able to be really honest and open with each other, which is so much like a romantic relationship in lots of ways.

Lauren: You've worked with long-time friends King Krule, James Blake and Micachu on this album. I'd love to talk about working with Mica Levi from Micachu and the Shapes. Her output is quite prolific, including film scores, and I think she's Oscar-nominated for one of them. Can you tell us about your working relationship and friendship with Micachu, and what she brought to this record?

Kai: She is probably the artist working today that's been the biggest influence on me. I think she's an incredible writer of music of all different types. The soundtrack stuff and score-based music is one thing, and then there's another part of her output with Micachu and the Shapes, which is just pure pop music, as I understand it. There is a purity to it that I find really exciting and refreshing and incredibly inspiring. I am a massive, massive fan of her.

I would occasionally bump into her at gigs in London. It's actually a fairly small world over here in music. I would always say something incredibly stupid because I was very nervous about what I was going to say to her. She would look at me funny and then I would walk off or something like that. But she was always really nice and generous about what we were doing.

Then she came in to have a listen to some stuff and have a chat at my old studio in Tottenham, and heard the first little loop of 'Marilyn' that I'd done and said it was something she felt like she would have ideas for. She got a piece of paper and wrote down some lyrics and recorded it in about two or three takes of lots of ideas, ad-libbing over it.

For someone who just sat down and wrote it, I think music just comes out of her. She's unlocked some secret level of creativity where she can write lyrics like the ones on 'Marilyn', which is so dense with imagery and ideas, and at the same time it's really, really simple. It's just a really, really great skill.

Lauren: You've mentioned that you're interested in things that are concise and prefer simple ideas over complicated ones. I remember talking to James Blake about simplicity, particularly the importance of space in his music and letting music breathe. I know the energy of the tracks is important to Mount Kimbie, particularly on this release. Is space within music something you relate to and try to achieve?

Kai: When a song or idea goes to the next level, suddenly it has this space where it has almost laws of physics inside it. It's like, "Well, it wouldn't do that." If you dropped a ball from the top of the stairs, it wouldn't do that. Sometimes an idea becomes clear, like the rules of the idea, in that way. That's the exciting part, because it's never as boring as gravity.

But I guess for this record, it's about trying to explore new— I mean, that is just the biggest fucking cliché ever to come out of my mouth. But just find new areas, in terms of space, that would be interesting, and ones that I wasn't familiar with.

Lauren: For the recent four-part NTS residency, you were split between LA and London, each hosting a couple of shows with life-size cardboard cutouts of your missing other half. What happened with the life-size cutout of Dom? Do you still have this at home to keep you company?

Kai: I respectfully packed it up at the end of the show, and we took it to the pub, and then I brought it home. When Dom's come to visit, I put it in my front window of the house so he could see it when he was coming from down the road.

Evidently the one of me got tossed around the studio at NTS and used as some kind of fucking physical joke prop in a lot of Instagram pictures. That was one of the worst pictures of me I've ever seen taken.

Lauren: You had a stack of guests joining you on that residency. I had a listen back and it included Julia Holter, James Blake, Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, Warpaint and Connan Mockasin. How did you approach putting together those shows? Was it fun to share new discoveries?

Kai: With the people, it was pretty much a wish list, and everyone said yes. So it was fairly easy on that front. When Archy came in, he played for most of the show. That was my favourite one out of the lot because it had a really good feeling, like what you sometimes get from live radio that nothing else can do, really.
